title: Sensors
description: How strain gauges, RTDs, thermistors, thermocouples and light sensors turn a physical quantity into an electrical one, and how to read them without loading.

study.title: Sensors and measurands
study.body:
A **sensor** turns a physical quantity, the **measurand** $m$, into an electrical quantity: a voltage, a current or a change in resistance, capacitance or inductance. Ideally the output is proportional to the measurand with sensitivity $K$ (e.g. V/N for a load cell).
Examples: temperature $\to$ thermocouple, RTD, thermistor; force $\to$ load cell (strain gauges); light $\to$ photodiode, LDR; displacement $\to$ LVDT, potentiometer; proximity $\to$ Hall-effect sensor.

study.title: Strain gauges
study.body: A strain gauge is a thin metal-foil resistor bonded to a part. When the part is stretched by strain $\varepsilon = \Delta L/L$, the gauge gets longer and thinner and its resistance rises. The **gauge factor** $G$ (about 2 for metal foil) links the two. Strains are tiny (typically below 0.002, written in µε = $10^{-6}$), so $\Delta R$ is a fraction of an ohm and is read with a bridge (next unit).

study.title: RTDs and thermistors
study.body:
An **RTD** (resistance temperature detector, usually platinum) has a resistance that rises almost linearly with temperature; $R = R_0(1+\alpha T)$; for a Pt100, $R_0$ = 100 Ω at 0 °C and $\alpha$ = 0.00385 /°C.
An **NTC thermistor** is a semiconductor whose resistance falls steeply and nonlinearly with temperature (temperatures in kelvin in the formula): much more sensitive, but less linear and over a smaller range.

study.title: Thermocouples
study.body: Two different metals joined at a hot junction produce a small voltage (**Seebeck effect**) proportional to the temperature **difference** between the hot junction and the reference (cold) junction where the wires meet the copper of the instrument. The Seebeck coefficient $S$ is tens of µV/°C (about 41 µV/°C for type K). The reference temperature must be measured separately: **cold-junction compensation**.

study.title: Light sensors
study.body:
A reverse-biased **photodiode** produces a current proportional to the light power: $i_D = \mathcal{R}P$ with responsivity $\mathcal{R}$ ≈ 0.5 A/W. To keep its voltage constant it feeds a **current-to-voltage converter** (transimpedance amplifier) with nearly zero input resistance: $v_o = -R_f i_D$.
An **LDR** (photoconductive cell) is a resistor whose resistance drops as the light gets brighter; it is slow but cheap.

study.title: Sensor loading
study.body:
Model a voltage-output sensor as a Thévenin source $v_{sensor}$ with resistance $R_{sensor}$. The amplifier's input resistance $R_{in}$ forms a voltage divider with it, so the amplifier sees less than $v_{sensor}$, and the loss changes whenever $R_{sensor}$ changes.
Voltage-output sensors need $R_{in} \gg R_{sensor}$; current-output sensors (photodiodes) need $R_{in} \approx 0$.

steps.title: What a sensor does
steps.body: A **sensor** converts the quantity we want to know, the **measurand**, into an electrical signal. Many sensors give a voltage proportional to the measurand; the constant $K$ is the **sensitivity**. Others change a resistance or produce a current that a signal conditioner turns into a voltage.

steps.prompt: Match each measurand to a typical sensor
steps.explanation: A thermocouple produces a temperature-dependent voltage, a load cell uses strain gauges on a loaded element, a photodiode gives a current proportional to light, an LVDT (linear variable differential transformer) senses core position, and a Hall sensor responds to a magnetic field.

steps.title: Strain gauges
steps.body: Stretching a metal-foil gauge by a strain $\varepsilon = \Delta L/L$ increases its resistance. The gauge factor $G$ (≈ 2) is the ratio of relative resistance change to strain. Strains are tiny: 1000 µε = 0.001 = 0.1 %.

steps.prompt: A {{R|Ω}} strain gauge with gauge factor {{G}} is stretched by {{u}} µε. Find the change in its resistance.
steps.explanation: $\Delta R = G\varepsilon R$ = {{G}} × {{u}} × $10^{-6}$ × {{R|Ω}} = **{{G*u*1e-6*R|Ω}}**, only {{G*u*1e-4|%}} of $R$. That is why gauges are read with a bridge and an amplifier.

steps.title: Resistance thermometers
steps.body: A platinum **RTD** increases its resistance almost linearly with temperature. The common Pt100 has $R_0$ = 100 Ω at 0 °C and $\alpha$ = 0.00385 per °C, so it changes by 0.385 Ω/°C. A **thermistor** is far more sensitive but strongly nonlinear.

steps.prompt: A platinum RTD has $R_0$ = {{R0|Ω}} at 0 °C and $\alpha$ = 0.00385 /°C. Find its resistance at {{T}} °C.
A temperature sensor has the resistance–temperature characteristic below. What kind of sensor is it?
steps.explanation: The resistance **falls** steeply and nonlinearly (from about 34 kΩ to below 1 kΩ) as the temperature rises: a negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) thermistor. A platinum RTD would be a nearly straight, slowly **rising** line, and a thermocouple produces a voltage, not a resistance.

steps.title: Thermocouples and photodiodes
steps.body:
A **thermocouple** gives a voltage proportional to the temperature difference between its hot junction and the reference (cold) junction, with a Seebeck coefficient $S$ of tens of µV/°C.
A **photodiode** gives a **current** proportional to light power. It is read with a current-to-voltage converter whose input resistance is nearly zero.

steps.prompt: A thermocouple with $S$ = {{S}} µV/°C has its hot junction at {{Th}} °C and its reference junction at {{Tr}} °C. Find its output voltage.
steps.explanation: $v = S(T_{hot} - T_{ref})$ = {{S}} µV/°C × ({{Th}} − {{Tr}}) °C = **{{S*1e-6*(Th-Tr)|V}}**. Only the temperature **difference** counts.

steps.prompt: A photodiode should be connected to an amplifier with a very **high** input resistance, so it is not loaded.
steps.explanation: A photodiode is a **current** source: its current is proportional to light only if its voltage stays constant. It therefore needs a current-to-voltage converter with nearly **zero** input resistance. High input resistance is what voltage-output sensors need.

steps.prompt: A platinum RTD ($R_0$ = {{R0|Ω}} at 0 °C, $\alpha$ = 0.00385 /°C) measures {{Rm||5}} Ω. What is the temperature in °C?
A {{R|Ω}} strain gauge with gauge factor {{G}} changes by +{{dR*1000||3}} mΩ under load. Find the strain (type e.g. 850u for 850 µε).
steps.explanation: $\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta R/R}{G}$ = ({{dR|Ω}} / {{R|Ω}}) / {{G}} = **{{dR/(G*R)|m/m}}** = {{dR/(G*R)*1e6||3}} µε (tension, since $R$ increased).

steps.prompt: A thermocouple with $S$ = {{S}} µV/°C reads {{v||4}} mV. A sensor at the reference junction shows {{Tr}} °C. Find the hot-junction temperature.
steps.explanation: $T_{hot} = T_{ref} + \frac{v}{S}$ = {{Tr}} °C + {{v||4}} mV / {{S}} µV/°C = {{Tr}} + {{v*1000/S||4}} = **{{Tr+v*1000/S||4}} °C**. Forgetting the reference junction would give only {{v*1000/S||4}} °C.

steps.prompt: An NTC thermistor has $R_{25}$ = 10 kΩ at 25 °C and $\beta$ = {{b}} K. Find its resistance at {{T}} °C, using $R = R_{25}\,e^{\beta(1/T - 1/T_{25})}$ with temperatures in kelvin.
A sensor with internal voltage $V_{sensor}$ and resistance $R_{sensor}$ drives an amplifier with input resistance $R_{in}$.

ask.prompt: By what percentage is the signal reduced by loading?

steps.prompt: A photodiode with responsivity {{Rl}} A/W receives {{P|W}} of light. Its current $i_D$ feeds the ideal current-to-voltage converter shown. Find $v_o$.
steps.explanation: $i_D = \mathcal{R}P$ = {{Rl}} A/W × {{P|W}} = {{Rl*P|A}}. The − input is a virtual ground, so all of $i_D$ flows through $R_f$ towards the output: $v_o = -R_f\,i_D$ = −{{Rf|Ω}} × {{Rl*P|A}} = **{{V_U1|V}}**.

steps.prompt: A platinum RTD ($R_0$ = {{R0|Ω}}, $\alpha$ = 0.00385 /°C) is excited by a constant current of {{I|A}}. Find the sensitivity of its voltage to temperature (volts per °C).
steps.explanation: $v = I R_0(1 + \alpha T)$, so $\frac{dv}{dT} = I\,\alpha R_0$ = {{I|A}} × 0.00385 × {{R0|Ω}} = **{{I*0.00385*R0|V/°C}}**. More current means more signal, but also more self-heating of the sensor.

steps.prompt: Match each sensor to the electrical quantity it changes or produces
steps.explanation: A thermocouple generates a voltage, a photodiode a current, an RTD changes its resistance and a level probe changes its capacitance as the liquid replaces air between the plates. Resistance and capacitance sensors need an excitation source to produce a voltage.

steps.prompt: An NTC thermistor ($R_{25}$ = 10 kΩ at 25 °C, $\beta$ = {{b}} K) measures {{Rm|Ω}}. Find the temperature in °C.

The resistance of a strain gauge (gauge factor {{G}}) also changes with temperature, with coefficient {{a*1e6}} ppm/°C. The unloaded part warms by {{dT}} °C. What strain would be wrongly indicated? (type e.g. 100u)
steps.explanation: Temperature gives $\frac{\Delta R}{R} = \alpha\Delta T$ = {{a*dT*1e6||3}} ppm. The instrument interprets this as $\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta R/R}{G}$ = **{{a*dT/G|m/m}}** ({{a*dT/G*1e6||3}} µε), comparable to real strains. A second, unstrained gauge in the bridge cancels this.

steps.prompt: A sensor's internal resistance varies between {{Ra|Ω}} and {{Rb|Ω}}. Find the minimum amplifier input resistance so that the overall sensitivity changes by no more than {{e}} % over this range.
steps.explanation: Sensitivity is proportional to $\frac{R_{in}}{R_{in}+R_s}$. Require $\frac{R_{in}}{R_{in}+R_b} \ge (1-\varepsilon)\frac{R_{in}}{R_{in}+R_a}$, i.e. $R_{in} + R_a \ge (1-\varepsilon)(R_{in}+R_b)$, so $R_{in} \ge \frac{(1-\varepsilon)R_b - R_a}{\varepsilon}$ = ({{(1-e/100)*Rb|Ω}} − {{Ra|Ω}}) / {{e/100||3}} = **{{((1-e/100)*Rb-Ra)/(e/100)|Ω}}**.

steps.prompt: A photodiode (responsivity {{Rl}} A/W) feeds a current-to-voltage converter. Choose $R_f$ so that the maximum light power of {{Pm|W}} gives an output magnitude of {{V|V}}.
steps.explanation: Maximum current: $i = \mathcal{R}P$ = {{Rl}} × {{Pm|W}} = {{Rl*Pm|A}}. $|v_o| = R_f i$, so $R_f$ = {{V|V}} / {{Rl*Pm|A}} = **{{V/(Rl*Pm)|Ω}}**.

steps.prompt: A platinum RTD ($R_0$ = {{R0|Ω}}, $\alpha$ = 0.00385 /°C) is connected with two copper leads of {{r|Ω}} each and read as a plain 2-wire resistance. How large is the resulting temperature error?
steps.explanation: The meter sees the sensor plus both leads: an extra {{2*r|Ω}}. The RTD changes by $\alpha R_0$ = {{0.00385*R0|Ω}} per °C, so the reading is too high by {{2*r|Ω}} / {{0.00385*R0||3}} Ω/°C = **{{2*r/(0.00385*R0)||3}} °C**. Use 3- or 4-wire connections (or a Pt1000) to avoid this.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the calibration of a pressure sensor. Find its sensitivity (volts per kPa).
steps.explanation: Sensitivity is the **slope**, not $v/p$ at one point (the line has an offset of {{V0|V}} at zero pressure). From 0 to 50 kPa the output goes from {{V0|V}} to {{V0+50*K|V}}: $K$ = ({{V0+50*K|V}} − {{V0|V}}) / 50 kPa = **{{K|V/kPa}}**.

steps.prompt: Compared with a platinum RTD, an NTC thermistor is much more sensitive (larger relative resistance change per °C) but much less linear.
steps.explanation: A Pt RTD changes by about 0.4 % per °C, almost linearly. An NTC thermistor changes by about −4 % per °C near room temperature, but exponentially, so it needs linearisation and works over a smaller range.
